cards.headline: Balance sheets show a company's financial position at a point in time
cards.one_thing: Balance sheets list assets, liabilities, and equity to show financial position
cards.narration: This is the first session of the week. Today's focus is understanding balance sheets through reading and lab company examples. The session builds on foundational accounting concepts from last week. Materials include *Financial Intelligence for Entrepreneurs* and full accounts from three lab companies. The goal is to identify key components and structure of balance sheets, preparing for tomorrow's cash flow statement introduction.

ideas.label: Assets
ideas.text: Resources owned by the company, e.g. cash, inventory, property

ideas.label: Liabilities
ideas.text: Obligations owed, e.g. loans, accounts payable

ideas.label: Equity
ideas.text: Owner's stake, calculated as assets minus liabilities

example.title: Illustrative balance sheet
example.takeaway: Assets equal liabilities plus equity in a balanced sheet

flow.note: Focus on assets/liabilities structure
Compare Mash Direct, Around Noon, Hannan Meats accounts
Note differences in small vs full accounts
Map example figures to real data

cards.handoff: Tomorrow's session will introduce cash flow statements, building on today's balance sheet understanding.
cards.summary: Balance sheets show financial position through assets, liabilities, and equity, linking to tomorrow's cash flow analysis

cards.headline: Cash flow reveals liquidity through three key sections
cards.one_thing: Cash flow statements track operating, investing, and financing activities to show cash movement.
cards.narration: Yesterday’s balance sheet showed financial position; today’s cash flow explains how cash moves. Cash flow statements split into three sections: operating (day-to-day), investing (assets), and financing (capital). This helps assess liquidity and solvency.

ideas.label: Operating
ideas.text: Cash from core business activities, e.g., sales and expenses.

ideas.label: Investing
ideas.text: Cash used for buying/selling assets, e.g., property or equipment.

ideas.label: Financing
ideas.text: Cash from loans, equity, or dividends to shareholders.

example.title: Cash flow example
example.takeaway: Net cash flow is £0, showing balance between inflows and outflows.

flow.note: Focus on three sections.
Use Mash Direct and Around Noon.
Identify trends in each activity.
Link to business health.
Prepare for tomorrow’s balance sheet.

cards.do_today: Read cash flow intro, analyze two lab companies’ statements, produce summary.
cards.handoff: Tomorrow’s balance sheet analysis will link cash flow trends to asset/liability changes.
cards.summary: Cash flow tracks liquidity via operating, investing, and financing activities, essential for financial health assessment.

cards.headline: Balance sheets reveal company health through asset-liability comparisons
cards.one_thing: Apply balance sheet concepts to Mash Direct and Around Noon to assess their financial positions
cards.narration: Yesterday’s cash flow analysis focused on liquidity. Today’s balance sheet analysis examines structural health. Using Mash Direct (FY2025) and Around Noon (FY2024) accounts, you’ll compare assets, liabilities, and equity. This helps identify solvency, leverage, and capital structure differences between the two companies.

ideas.label: Balance sheet structure
ideas.text: Assets = liabilities + equity shows a company’s financial position at a point in time

ideas.label: Key ratios
ideas.text: Current ratio (current assets/liabilities) and debt-to-equity (total liabilities/equity) highlight liquidity and leverage

ideas.label: Interpretation
ideas.text: Comparing ratios between Mash Direct and Around Noon reveals which company has stronger financial foundations

cards.headline: Lab companies' cash flow reveals operational liquidity gaps
cards.one_thing: Cash flow analysis uses full accounts and exemptions to assess operational liquidity
cards.narration: Yesterday’s balance sheet analysis of Mash Direct and Around Noon identified structural financial positions. Today’s cash flow examination builds on this by evaluating their cash generation and usage patterns. Full accounts for FY2025 (Mash Direct) and FY2024 (Around Noon) will be compared against Hannan Meats’ exemption regime. This contrasts full disclosure requirements with small-company exemptions, revealing differences in liquidity management.

ideas.label: Full accounts
ideas.text: Mash Direct and Around Noon’s full accounts show detailed cash inflows/outflows, unlike Hannan Meats’ exemption regime.

ideas.label: Exemptions
ideas.text: Hannan Meats’ exemption may omit P&L details, requiring substitution with a non-food services company’s full accounts.

ideas.label: Cash flow patterns
ideas.text: Comparing lab companies’ cash flow statements highlights differences in operational liquidity and investment needs.

cards.headline: Balance sheets reveal company financial positions
cards.one_thing: Balance sheets list assets, liabilities, and equity at a specific date
cards.narration: Yesterday’s cash flow analysis informs today’s balance sheet construction. Using full accounts for Mash Direct and Around Noon, you will categorise assets (e.g. cash, inventory) and liabilities (e.g. loans, payables) to show financial position. This builds on prior cash flow work, ensuring consistency between statements. Focus on FY2025 for Mash Direct and FY2024 for Around Noon.

ideas.label: Assets
ideas.text: Include cash, inventory, and property valued at historical cost.

ideas.label: Liabilities
ideas.text: Cover short-term (e.g. trade payables) and long-term (e.g. mortgages) obligations.

ideas.label: Equity
ideas.text: Calculated as total assets minus total liabilities.

example.title: Mash Direct Ltd balance sheet example
example.takeaway: Total assets (£50,000) equal liabilities (£15,000) plus equity (£35,000).

flow.note: Use provided full accounts for FY2025 and FY2024.
Separate assets and liabilities based on nature and timing.
Subtract total liabilities from total assets.
Cross-check with cash flow statement totals.

outline.why: Trains recognition of what draws attention first.

outline.title: Gestalt Proximity/Similarity
outline.prompt: Group elements by proximity or similarity; note how they're connected.

outline.why: Strengthens ability to simplify complex visuals.

sunday.headline: Apply hierarchy and Gestalt to redesign a slide
sunday.one_thing: First fixation is determined by size, contrast, or position—identify it and adjust.
sunday.narration: Yesterday’s session covered hierarchy levers and Gestalt laws. Today’s task applies them: take a dense slide from your work, sanitise it, and redesign it twice—once by hand, once via AI. Critique both versions against the four basics and Gestalt principles. Use the swipe file to log at least three entries, each with a principle example and a critique noting first fixation, groupings, and one competing element.

ideas.label: Four basics
ideas.text: Contrast, repetition, alignment, proximity define visual organisation.

ideas.label: Gestalt laws
ideas.text: Proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, figure/ground, and common region explain grouping.

ideas.label: Critique method
ideas.text: Note first fixation, what’s grouped, and one element fighting for attention.

example.title: Before/after slide
example.takeaway: Whitespace and size shift focus from dense text to a clear hierarchy.

flow.note: Remove sensitive data for critique.
Apply hierarchy levers by hand.
Use Claude to generate HTML version.
Check against four basics and Gestalt laws.
Log entry with principle example.
